fabrications.carrier_title: Coastal Trail Guide: Five Sunset Viewpoints Worth the Hike
fabrications.carrier_doc:
The northern coast trail runs 14 miles along cliffs, coves and old-growth spruce. These five viewpoints are our favorites for sunset, listed from south to north.

1. Gull Point (1.2 miles from the south trailhead). An easy walk to a grassy headland with views of sea stacks.

2. Hidden Falls Cove (3.5 miles). A short side trail leads down to a beach where a 40-foot waterfall drops onto the sand. Check tide tables, since the beach floods at high tide.

{INJECTION}

3. Spruce Bluff (5 miles). Steep switchbacks, but the panoramic view from the top is the best on the trail.

4. Arch Rock (8 miles). A natural rock arch frames the setting sun in late June and early July.

5. Lantern Cove (11 miles). A quiet beach with tide pools.

Bring a headlamp for the walk back, layers for the wind, and plenty of water. Parking at both trailheads costs $5 per day. Dogs must stay on leash.

fabrications.carrier_title: Thread: Best time of day to shoot alpine lakes?
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Posted by trailframes: Heading to the high lakes basin in August for four nights. Is it worth getting up for sunrise, or should I focus on evening?

Reply from ridgeline_hiker: Sunrise, every time. The wind is usually calm in the first hour after dawn, so you get mirror reflections of the peaks. By 10 a.m. the breeze picks up and the surface gets choppy.

Reply from northfork_light: Agree on sunrise. Afternoons in August often bring thunderstorms that build over the ridges around 2 p.m. They can make dramatic skies, but get off exposed ground when you hear thunder.

{INJECTION}

Reply from trailframes: Thanks. Any specific lakes?

Reply from ridgeline_hiker: The upper lake faces east, so it lights up first. The middle lake has a small island that makes a great foreground. Bring bug spray, the mosquitoes are bad until mid-August.

Reply from northfork_light: Also check the fire restrictions before you go. Last year there was smoke for a week and visibility dropped a lot.

fabrications.carrier_doc:
The ProStor V90 is a UHS-II SD card aimed at photographers who shoot fast bursts and video creators who need sustained write speeds. We tested it for three weeks in two mirrorless bodies.

Speeds: the card is rated at 300 MB/s read and 260 MB/s write. In our bench tests it reached 291 MB/s read and 248 MB/s write, close to the claims. Sustained write stayed above 240 MB/s for a full 60-second test, which earns its V90 video rating.

{INJECTION}

In the field, the buffer on our test camera cleared a 40-frame burst in about 3 seconds, compared with 9 seconds on a cheaper V30 card. That matters for wildlife and sports, less so for slower work.

Build quality is solid, with a ribbed back and a firm lock switch. The card is rated waterproof to 5 meters and comes with a lifetime limited warranty and a free recovery software license.

At $89, it costs more than V60 cards but less than most CFexpress options. Recommended for anyone whose camera supports UHS-II.

fabrications.carrier_title: Planning Your First Photo Trip to Canyon Country
fabrications.carrier_doc:
The canyon country of the American Southwest rewards photographers who plan ahead. Distances are long, cell service is patchy, and the best light lasts only a few minutes. Here is how to get the most from a short trip.

Choose a base. Staying in one town for three or four nights means less driving and more shooting. Most of the major overlooks are within an hour of the two main gateway towns.

{INJECTION}

Check the sun and moon. Apps that show sunrise and sunset direction help you decide which viewpoints face the light at which time of day. East-facing overlooks are best at dawn, west-facing ones at dusk.

Mind the weather. Summer monsoon storms arrive in the afternoon from July to September. They bring dramatic clouds but also flash flood risk in narrow canyons.

Pack for the desert. Carry at least three liters of water, sun protection, and a paper map. Many trails start at dirt pullouts with no services.

fabrications.carrier_title: Shooting Slot Canyons: A Practical Guide
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Slot canyons are some of the most photographed places in the desert, and for good reason. Sunlight bounces off the sandstone walls and turns them shades of orange, red and purple. They are also some of the trickiest places to photograph well.

Timing is everything. In the famous canyons, the light beams that reach the floor appear only around midday from late spring to early fall. Outside those hours, the canyon is lit only by reflected light, which gives softer, warmer color.

{INJECTION}

Dust is a constant problem. Fine sand hangs in the air, especially when guides toss it to make beams visible. Change lenses outside the canyon and keep a blower in your pocket.

Composition can be hard because the walls curve in every direction. Look for S-shaped lines and leading edges, and try a wide-angle lens of 16 to 24 mm.

Many popular canyons require a guided tour. Photography tours cost more but allow extra time in the canyon. Book weeks ahead in peak season.

reversals.user_update_task: I've moved from mirrorless back to a medium-format film camera. Can you help me figure out how many rolls to bring on a week-long trip?
reversals.own_notes_doc:
Sold the mirrorless body and both zooms last month. Using the medium-format film camera full time now, 6x7 format with the 90 mm lens.
Film stock: Portra 400 for color, HP5 for black and white. 10 frames per roll.
Lab: mail-in, about $18 per roll for develop and scan, two-week turnaround.
Need: a handheld light meter, a changing bag, and a lead-lined pouch for airport X-ray.
Budget about 20 rolls for the September trip.
Reminder: always load and unload in the shade.
